Choosing a D&D gift for a player or game master

By Couple Better Gifts · Updated October 19, 2026 · How we choose gifts

Ask whether they play a character, run the game, or do both. Then find out whether the group meets around a table or plays online. These two questions help you choose between character accessories, campaign tools, and physical pieces they will actually use.

Buying a rulebook: confirm the version

The 2014 and 2024 Player’s Handbook contain different versions of the rules and character options. Ask which book their group uses and which specific title they want. D&D Beyond explains the revisions in its 2024 Player’s Handbook update.

Check the publication year and product format before ordering. Confirm whether they want a physical book, a digital purchase for their chosen platform, or a bundle. Also check that they do not already own it. Apply the same rules-version check to formatted character journals and reference cards.

Dice: make the numbers easy to read

The official D&D Basic Rules describe dice including d4, d6, d8, d10, d12, and d20. Read the set’s contents and look closely at the number contrast. A decorative pattern can make the values difficult to distinguish.

Consider the material and the surface where they roll. Heavy dice may call for a lined tray. If they already collect dice, ask about colors or materials they like; if they usually roll digitally, a physical set may see little use.

Match the gift to the session

GiftUseful forCheck first
Character journalA player who likes handwritten notes.Rules version and page layout.
Campaign notebookA game master keeping session and world notes.Writing space and their existing system.
Dice bagSomeone who carries dice between games.Capacity and closure.
Folding dice trayA player with room for a rolling area.Open dimensions and packed size.
MiniatureA group that uses physical figures.Character, scale, and painting preference.

Miniatures: check the work involved

Ask whether their group uses miniatures and whether the recipient enjoys painting. An unpainted figure requires time and supplies. Read what is included: paints, brushes, bases, and glue may be separate purchases. Check the model’s size against pieces they already use.

A game master may already have a collection suited to a campaign. Ask which creatures or characters would help before buying a large assorted set. For character merchandise, check the maker’s licensing information and choose an identifiable seller.

If you cannot confirm those details, a flexible notebook gives them room for their own system. Add a note explaining which campaign or character made you think of them.
